title: VII. The Second Visit To Smerdyakov
paragraphs: By this time Smerdyakov had been discharged from the hospital. Ivan knew his new lodgings, the run-down little wooden house divided in two by a hallway, with Marya Kondratyevna and her mother living on one side and Smerdyakov on the other. No one knew exactly on what terms he lived with them—whether as a friend or a lodger. It was assumed afterward that he'd moved in as Marya Kondratyevna's fiancé, and was living there for the time being without paying for room or board. Both mother and daughter held him in the highest respect and considered him far above themselves.

Ivan knocked, and when the door opened, went straight into the hallway. Following Marya Kondratyevna's directions, he went straight to the better room on the left, the one Smerdyakov occupied. There was a tiled stove in the room, and it was extremely hot. The walls were done in cheerful blue paper, though quite worn, and in the cracks beneath it cockroaches swarmed in astonishing numbers, so that there was a constant rustling sound. The furniture was sparse: two benches along the walls and two chairs by the table. The plain wooden table was covered with a cloth patterned in pink. There was a pot of geraniums on each of the two small windows. In the corner stood a case of icons. On the table sat a little copper samovar, badly dented, and a tray with two cups. But Smerdyakov had already finished his tea and the samovar had gone cold. He was sitting at the table on a bench, looking at a notebook and writing slowly with a pen. There was a bottle of ink beside him and a flat iron candlestick holding a composite candle. Ivan could see at once from Smerdyakov's face that he'd fully recovered from his illness. His face was fresher, fuller; his hair stood up jauntily in front and was slicked down at the sides. He sat in a multicolored, padded dressing gown, though fairly dirty and frayed. He had spectacles on his nose, which Ivan had never seen him wear before. This trivial detail suddenly doubled Ivan's anger: a creature like that, wearing spectacles!

Smerdyakov slowly raised his head and looked intently at his visitor through his spectacles; then he slowly took them off and got up from the bench, though by no means respectfully—almost lazily, doing the bare minimum that ordinary politeness demanded. Ivan took all this in at once, noting every bit of it—above all the look in Smerdyakov's eyes, genuinely malicious, sullen, and haughty. "What are you barging in here for?" it seemed to say. "We settled everything already; why have you come again?" Ivan could barely control himself.
"It's hot in here," he said, still standing, and unbuttoned his overcoat.
"Take your coat off," Smerdyakov conceded.
Ivan took off his coat and tossed it onto a bench with trembling hands. He grabbed a chair, pulled it up to the table, and sat down. Smerdyakov managed to get himself seated on his bench before him.
"First of all—are we alone here?" Ivan asked, sharp and abrupt. "Can they hear us from in there?"
"No one can hear a thing. You saw for yourself—there's a hallway."

"Listen, my good man—what was that you were mumbling as I was leaving the hospital, that if I kept quiet about your talent for faking fits, you wouldn't tell the investigating lawyer all about our conversation at the gate? What do you mean by all? What were you getting at? Were you threatening me? Have I made some kind of deal with you? Do you think I'm afraid of you?"

Ivan said all this in an absolute fury, making it plain, with obvious intent, that he despised any evasion or indirectness and meant to lay his cards on the table. Smerdyakov's eyes gleamed with resentment, his left eye twitched, and he gave his answer at once, with his usual composure and deliberateness. "You want everything out in the open? Fine, you'll have it," he seemed to be saying.

"What I meant then, and why I said it, was that you, knowing beforehand about this murder of your own father, left him to his fate—and that people, after that, might draw all sorts of conclusions about your feelings, and about something else too. That's what I promised not to tell the authorities."

Though Smerdyakov spoke without hurrying, clearly holding himself in check, there was something in his voice—firm and pointed, resentful and insolently defiant. He stared at Ivan with open impudence. For a moment everything blurred before Ivan's eyes.
"How's that? What? Have you lost your mind?"
"I'm in full possession of all my faculties."
"Do you imagine I knew about the murder?" Ivan finally shouted, slamming his fist on the table. "What do you mean by 'something else too'? Speak, you scoundrel!"
Smerdyakov stayed silent, still fixing Ivan with the same insolent stare.
"Speak, you stinking wretch—what's this 'something else too'?"
"By 'something else,' I meant that you, too, probably wanted your father dead."

Ivan jumped up and struck him with all his strength on the shoulder, knocking him back against the wall. In an instant his face was streaming with tears. Saying, "It's shameful, sir, to strike a sick man," he wiped his eyes with a filthy blue checked handkerchief and sank into quiet weeping. A minute passed.
"That's enough! Stop," Ivan said sharply, sitting back down. "Don't push me past all patience."
Smerdyakov took the rag from his eyes. Every line of his creased face reflected the insult he'd just received.
"So you thought, then, you scoundrel, that I meant to kill my father together with Dmitri?"
"I didn't know what was in your mind at the time," Smerdyakov said resentfully, "so I stopped you there at the gate to sound you out on that exact point."
"Sound me out about what, what?"
"Why, that very thing—whether you wanted your father murdered or not."
What infuriated Ivan more than anything was the aggressive, insolent tone Smerdyakov kept up throughout.
"It was you who murdered him?" he suddenly cried.
Smerdyakov smiled contemptuously.
"You know for a fact yourself that it wasn't me who murdered him. And I'd have thought a sensible man wouldn't need to bring that up again."
"But why, why did you have such a suspicion about me at the time?"

"As you already know, it was simply out of fear. I was in such a state, shaking with fear, that I suspected everyone. I decided to sound you out too, because I thought if you wanted the same thing as your brother, then the matter was as good as settled, and I'd be crushed like a fly too."
"Look here—you didn't say any of that two weeks ago."

"I meant the same thing when I talked with you at the hospital, only I thought you'd understand without needing it spelled out, and that being such a sensible man, you wouldn't care to discuss it openly."
"What next! Come on, answer me, answer, I insist: what was it... what could I have done to put such a degrading suspicion into your low soul?"
"As for the murder itself, you couldn't have done it and didn't want to—but as for wanting someone else to do it, that's exactly what you did want."
"And how coolly, how coolly he says it! But why would I have wanted it? What grounds did I have for wanting it?"

"What grounds did you have? What about the inheritance?" Smerdyakov said, sarcastically, almost vindictively. "After your father's death, there'd have been at least forty thousand coming to each of you, likely more—but if Fyodor Pavlovitch had married that lady, Agrafena Alexandrovna, she'd have had all his capital signed over to her right after the wedding, because she's got plenty of sense, and your father wouldn't have left the three of you two roubles between you. And were they far from a wedding? Not by a hair—that lady only had to crook her little finger and he'd have gone running to church after her, tongue hanging out."
Ivan restrained himself with painful effort.
"Very good," he said at last. "You see, I haven't jumped up, I haven't knocked you down, I haven't killed you. Go on. So, according to you, I'd settled on Dmitri to do it—I was counting on him?"

"How could you not count on him? If he killed him, he'd lose every right of a nobleman, his rank, his property, and be sent off to exile—so his share of the inheritance would come to you and your brother Alexey Fyodorovitch, split in two. Each of you would get not forty, but sixty thousand. There's not a doubt you were counting on Dmitri Fyodorovitch."

"What I have to put up with from you! Listen, you scoundrel—if I'd counted on anyone at the time, it would have been you, not Dmitri, and I swear to you I did expect some piece of villainy from you... at the time.... I remember exactly what I felt!"

"I thought so too, for a minute, at the time—that you were counting on me as well," Smerdyakov said with a sarcastic grin. "And that's exactly how you showed me, more than anything, what was in your mind. Because if you had a premonition about me and still went off, it was as good as saying to me, 'You can go ahead and murder my father, I won't stop you!'"
"You scoundrel! So that's how you took it!"

"It was all that business with Tchermashnya. Think about it! You meant to go to Moscow and refused all your father's pleading to go to Tchermashnya instead—and then, on one foolish word from me, you agreed at once! What reason did you have to agree to Tchermashnya? Since you went to Tchermashnya for no reason at all, simply on my say-so, it shows you must have been expecting something from me."
"No, I swear I wasn't!" Ivan shouted, grinding his teeth.

"You weren't? Then, as your father's son, you should have had me hauled off to the lockup and beaten right then for saying that... or at the very least, punched me in the face on the spot. But you weren't the least bit angry, if you please—you went along with my foolish word right there in a friendly way and left, which was utterly absurd, because you should have stayed to save your father's life. How could I not draw my own conclusions?"
Ivan sat there scowling, both fists pressed convulsively against his knees.

"Yes, I'm sorry I didn't punch you in the face," he said, with a bitter smile. "I couldn't have had you hauled to the lockup just then—who would have believed me, and what charge could I have brought against you? But the punch in the face... oh, I'm sorry I didn't think of it. Even though blows are forbidden, I should have pounded your ugly face into pulp."
Smerdyakov looked at him with something like relish.

"In the ordinary run of life," he said, in the same self-satisfied, sententious tone he'd used to taunt Grigory and argue about religion at Fyodor Pavlovitch's table, "in the ordinary run of life, blows to the face are forbidden nowadays by law, and people have given them up. But in exceptional circumstances, people still resort to blows—not just among us, but all over the world, even in the fullest republic of France, exactly as in the days of Adam and Eve, and they never will stop doing it. But you, even in an exceptional case, didn't dare."
"What are you learning French words for?" Ivan nodded toward the notebook lying on the table.
"Why shouldn't I learn them, to improve my education, in case I might happen to go one day to those happy parts of Europe?"

"Listen, you monster." Ivan's eyes flashed and he trembled all over. "I'm not afraid of your accusations. Say what you like about me. And if I don't beat you to death, it's simply because I suspect you of that crime, and I'll drag you before the law. I'll expose you."

"If you ask me, you'd do better to stay quiet, because what can you accuse me of, given my complete innocence? And who would believe you? Only, if you start, I'll tell everything too, since I have to defend myself."
"Do you think I'm afraid of you now?"
"If the court doesn't believe everything I've just told you, the public will, and you'll be disgraced."
"That's as much as to say, 'It's always worth talking to a sensible man,' isn't it?" Ivan snarled.
"You've hit it exactly. And you'd better be sensible."

Ivan got up, shaking all over with indignation, put on his coat, and without another word to Smerdyakov, without even looking at him, walked quickly out of the house. The cool evening air was a relief. A bright moon hung in the sky. A nightmare of thoughts and sensations filled his soul. "Should I go straight and report Smerdyakov? But what could I report? He's not guilty of anything, anyway. If anything, he'll accuse me. And really, why did I set off for Tchermashnya then? What for? What for?" Ivan asked himself. "Yes, of course—I was expecting something, and he's right...." And for the hundredth time he remembered how, on that last night in his father's house, he'd listened on the stairs. But he remembered it now with such anguish that he stopped dead where he stood, as though he'd been stabbed. "Yes, I expected it then, that's true! I wanted the murder, I did want it! Did I want the murder? Did I want it? I have to kill Smerdyakov! If I don't dare kill Smerdyakov now, life isn't worth living!"

Ivan didn't go home, but went straight to Katerina Ivanovna's, and alarmed her with his appearance. He looked like a madman. He repeated his whole conversation with Smerdyakov, word for word. Nothing she tried could calm him: he kept pacing the room, talking strangely, disjointedly. At last he sat down, put his elbows on the table, leaned his head on his hands, and pronounced this strange sentence: "If it's not Dmitri, but Smerdyakov, who's the murderer, then I share his guilt, because I put him up to it. Whether I did—I don't know yet. But if he's the murderer, and not Dmitri, then of course I'm the murderer too."

When Katerina Ivanovna heard this, she rose from her seat without a word, went to her writing table, opened a box sitting on it, took out a sheet of paper, and laid it before Ivan. This was the document Ivan later spoke of to Alyosha as "conclusive proof" that Dmitri had killed his father. It was the letter Mitya had written to Katerina Ivanovna while drunk, on that very evening he'd met Alyosha at the crossroads on the way to the monastery, right after the scene at Katerina Ivanovna's, when Grushenka had insulted her. After leaving Alyosha, Mitya had rushed off to Grushenka. I don't know whether he saw her, but that evening he was at the Metropolis, where he got thoroughly drunk. Then he'd asked for pen and paper and written a document that would carry heavy consequences for him. It was a rambling, disjointed, frantic letter—a drunken letter, in fact. It read like the talk of a drunk man who, coming home, launches with tremendous heat into telling his wife or someone in his household how he's just been insulted, what a scoundrel just insulted him, what a fine fellow he is by comparison, and how he'll pay that scoundrel back—all of it at enormous length, worked up and incoherent, with drunken tears and pounding on the table. The letter was written on a dirty piece of cheap ordinary paper, supplied by the tavern, with some figures scrawled on the back. There clearly wasn't enough space for his drunken outpouring, and Mitya had filled not only the margins but written his last line straight across the rest of the text. The letter read as follows:

FATAL KATYA: Tomorrow I'll get the money and pay back your three thousand, and farewell, woman of great wrath—but farewell, too, my love! Let's put an end to it! Tomorrow I'll try to get it from everyone, and if I can't borrow it, I give you my word of honor I'll go to my father, break his skull, and take the money out from under his pillow, so long as Ivan's gone by then. Even if it means Siberia, I'll pay back your three thousand. And farewell. I bow down to the ground before you, because I've been a scoundrel to you. Forgive me! No—better not forgive me, you'll be happier, and so will I! Better Siberia than your love, because I love another woman, and you got to know her far too well today, so how could you forgive me? I'll murder the man who's robbed me! I'll leave you all and go east, so I never see anyone again. Not her either, because you're not my only tormentor—she is too. Farewell! P.S. I write my curse, but I adore you! I feel it in my heart. One string is left, and it's still vibrating. Better to tear my heart in two! I'll kill myself, but first, that cur. I'll tear three thousand out of him and throw it at your feet. Though I've been a scoundrel to you, I'm not a thief! You can count on the three thousand. The cur keeps it under his mattress, tied with pink ribbon. I'm not a thief, but I'll murder my thief. Katya, don't look at me with contempt. Dmitri is no thief! But a murderer! He'll murder his father and destroy himself to hold his ground, rather than endure your pride. And he doesn't love you. P.P.S. I kiss your feet, farewell! P.P.P.S. Katya, pray to God someone gives me the money. Then I won't be drenched in blood—and if no one does, I will be! Kill me!
Your slave and enemy, D. KARAMAZOV.

When Ivan read this "document," he was convinced. So it was his brother, then, not Smerdyakov. And if not Smerdyakov, then not him, Ivan. In his eyes the letter immediately took on the shape of logical proof. There could no longer be the slightest doubt of Mitya's guilt. It never occurred to Ivan, incidentally, that Mitya might have committed the murder together with Smerdyakov—and indeed, such a theory didn't fit the facts. Ivan was thoroughly reassured. The next morning he thought of Smerdyakov and his taunts only with contempt. A few days later he genuinely wondered how he could have been so horribly shaken by his own suspicions. He resolved to dismiss the man with contempt and forget him. A month went by like this. He made no further inquiries about Smerdyakov, though twice he happened to hear that he was very ill and out of his mind.

"He'll end up mad," the young doctor Varvinsky remarked about him, and Ivan remembered this. During the last week of that month Ivan himself began to feel quite ill. He went to consult the Moscow doctor Katerina Ivanovna had sent for just before the trial. And it was around this time that his relations with Katerina Ivanovna grew sharply strained. They were like two enemies in love with each other. Katerina Ivanovna's "returns" to Mitya—her brief but violent swings of feeling back in his favor—drove Ivan to a state of pure frenzy. Strangely enough, right up until that last scene described earlier, when Alyosha came from Mitya to Katerina Ivanovna's, Ivan had never once, during that entire month, heard her express any doubt of Mitya's guilt, despite those "returns" he found so hateful. It's worth noting, too, that while he felt his hatred of Mitya growing daily, he understood that it wasn't because of Katya's "returns" that he hated him, but simply because he was his father's murderer. He was conscious of this, and admitted it fully to himself.

Even so, he went to see Mitya ten days before the trial and proposed a plan of escape to him—a plan he'd clearly thought over for a long time. He was driven to it, in part, by a sore spot still lingering in his heart from a remark of Smerdyakov's: that it was to his, Ivan's, advantage that his brother be convicted, since that would raise his own and Alyosha's inheritance from forty to sixty thousand roubles. He decided to sacrifice thirty thousand toward arranging Mitya's escape. Coming back from that visit, he was deeply mournful and dejected; he suddenly began to sense that he was anxious for Mitya's escape not only to heal that sore spot by sacrificing thirty thousand, but for some other reason too. "Is it because I'm just as much a murderer at heart?" he asked himself. Something very deep down seemed to be burning and festering in his soul. His pride, above all, suffered cruelly that whole month. But more on that later....

When, after his conversation with Alyosha, Ivan suddenly decided, hand on the bell of his lodgings, to go see Smerdyakov instead, he was obeying a sudden, strange surge of indignation. He'd suddenly remembered how Katerina Ivanovna had just cried out to him, in front of Alyosha: "It was you, you, who convinced me of his"—meaning Mitya's—"guilt!" Ivan was thunderstruck, recalling it. He'd never once tried to convince her Mitya was the murderer; on the contrary, he'd suspected himself in front of her, that time when he came back from Smerdyakov's. It was she, she, who had produced that "document" and proved his brother's guilt. And now she'd suddenly cried out: "I've been to see Smerdyakov myself!" When had she gone there? Ivan had known nothing about it. So she wasn't at all so certain of Mitya's guilt after all! And what could Smerdyakov have told her? What, what had he said to her? His heart burned with furious anger. He couldn't understand how, half an hour earlier, he'd let those words slip past without crying out on the spot. He let go of the bell and rushed off toward Smerdyakov's. "Maybe I'll kill him this time," he thought, on the way.
